title: The persecution of 845
hook: a Tang emperor closes the monasteries; the teachings that needed little come through

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chan monastery, where Mazu and Baizhang shaped work, meals and sitting into one life. Your line was work is practice. Which chore did you turn into practice? Day nine hundred seventeen.

Bells are being lowered from temple towers and carted off to be melted down. Bronze images go into the furnaces after them. Monks and nuns are told to take off their robes and go home as ordinary subjects. The halls are emptied, the gates are shut. This is China under the Tang emperor Wuzong, and a monk from Japan, far from home, is watching it happen and writing it down in his diary, while he tries to get himself and his books out of the country. Today, the persecution of 845, and the question it leaves on the table: when the buildings go, what's left?
screen: `BELLS GO TO THE FURNACE.` → `ROBES COME OFF.` → `WHAT'S LEFT?`

segments.voice: First, the orders. The official histories of the Tang dynasty date the harshest of Emperor Wuzong's decrees to 845. The court had come to see the monasteries as a drain: land, metal and people outside the tax rolls, serving a teaching that came from abroad. Wuzong himself favored Daoist masters. His decrees closed monasteries across the empire and sent monks and nuns back to lay life. Second, the eyewitness. The monk from Japan was Ennin, and his diary of his years in China lets us see it from the road: monks forced into lay clothes, images stripped, foreign monks sent away. To get home, he put on ordinary clothes himself. Third, what came through. The worst of it was short; the histories tell that Wuzong died soon after, and the next emperor eased the ban. But schools that leaned on great libraries, rich estates and the court's favor were badly shaken. A common way of telling the story is that two schools came through more easily. Chan, whose monks, like Baizhang's, worked their own fields and taught face to face. And Pure Land, whose practice could be carried in a single breath: the name of Amitabha Buddha, said by anyone, anywhere, with no building at all. Fourth, the old teaching underneath. The Buddha taught that all conditioned things pass away. An empire can take bells, roofs and robes. It is much harder to confiscate a habit of sitting still, or a name a grandmother says over the stove. That closes a week that began with Bodhidharma facing a wall, a week of stories saying the teaching did not live in the buildings.
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S DECREES.` · `ENNIN'S DIARY SAW IT.` · `WHAT NEEDED LITTLE CAME THROUGH.` · `ALL CONDITIONED THINGS PASS.` · then, large: `WHAT SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor something that survived. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one thing that came through a hard time and reached you: a recipe in someone's handwriting, a song a parent sang, an old building on your street, a habit you kept through a bad year. Hold it in your attention. Notice what it needed in order to last, and what it turned out not to need. If you'd like, bow to it slightly, with your head or only in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Ennin. The Japanese monk whose diary recorded the closing of China's monasteries under Emperor Wuzong, in 845. Today's word.
Your line: what survived. Today, when you pass something old, a tree, a wall, a worn tool, stop for one breath and wonder what it came through. That's the week. Day nine hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Chinese Buddhists remember the persecution under Emperor Wuzong as one of the hard turns in their history, and Chan and Pure Land communities often tell it as part of their own story of carrying the teaching through.

fork.setup: you're a monk in China as the emperor's decrees arrive. your monastery is closing. what do you carry out with you?
options: the practice: sitting, working, a name you can say.
nothing; you give it all up.
fork.reveal: a common telling is that the schools that came through most easily were the ones that traveled light: Chan's sitting and fieldwork, Pure Land's spoken name.

original.note: Pali anicca: impermanent, the Buddha's word for how conditioned things pass.
